edbDesc: An instability of an interface between two fluids of different densities, which occurs when the lighter fluid is pushing the heavier fluid.
title: Rayleigh-Taylor instability
description: When a heavy fluid sits on a light one, or a light fluid pushes on a heavy one, the boundary can't stay flat: it grows fingers and mushroom shapes that sink and rise into each other. Lord Rayleigh worked it out in 1883 and G. I. Taylor extended it in 1950 to accelerating fluids. It is why water spills from an upside-down glass even though air pressure could hold it up, why big explosions make mushroom clouds, and the main thing laser-fusion fuel capsules must be designed to resist.
effect: a heavy fluid resting on a lighter one breaks into growing fingers and plumes
usedIn: Fuel-capsule design for laser fusion at the National Ignition Facility
Rising wax blobs in lava lamps
Simulations of supernovas and mushroom clouds
strength: Fast: ripples on the surface of water held upside down grow and spill in a fraction of a second; in a fusion capsule tiny ripples grow a thousandfold in billionths of a second.
pickWhy: Specific named effect; its job is mostly mixing and something to design against, but uses are imaginable. Canonical card for the family (Richtmyer-Meshkov merges here).
